page_title: Compressing Chess Moves for Fun and Profit

summary.title: Compressing Chess Moves for Fun and Profit
summary.one_liner: You learn how to pack Standard Algebraic Notation chess moves into a few bits each using piece, square, capture, and special-move encodings, shrinking a 759-byte PGN to about 195 bytes.
keywords: how many bits does a chess move need
takeaways: A chess move's information content is far below its text size: piece (3 bits), capture flag, and destination (6 bits) give about 10 bits for Qxf7 versus 32 bits as text.
Unused bit patterns can be reused, e.g. the two spare piece codes encode short and long castling.
Pawn moves need fewer destination bits, since the file is implied, and a 'special' flag lets regular moves use fewer bits.
Encoding a full PGN without separators reduced a 759-byte game to 195 bytes (74% savings), and encoding/decoding 1000 moves took about 0.6 ms in Rust with bitvec.
summary.summary: The author argues that SAN moves such as Qxf7 waste space and works out the real information content per move. They then build a bit-level encoding step by step: 3 bits for the piece with spare codes reused for castling, a destination square of 6 bits (fewer for pawn captures), a one-bit 'special' flag, and compact promotion and disambiguation codes. Results are tabulated for sample moves (savings of 37.5% to 71.43%), and the full PGN compresses by 74%. The post closes with a performance note using Rust and the bitvec crate, and it says the change was not yet deployed.
